questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Composition of a primary stem villus
questions.question: A primary stem villus consists of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Cytotrophoblast alone omits the syncytiotrophoblast, which is also present in a primary villus -- both trophoblast layers together, with no mesoderm, define this stage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Syncytiotrophoblast alone likewise omits the cytotrophoblast, also present in a primary villus.
explanations.C: Correct. A primary villus is trophoblast alone, made of cytotrophoblast plus syncytiotrophoblast. It has no mesenchymal core at all. This is the earliest villus stage, before any mesoderm has invaded it to form a secondary villus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adding extraembryonic mesoderm describes the secondary (not primary) villus stage, once mesoderm has invaded the trophoblastic core.
explanations.E: Incorrect. This combination both omits the cytotrophoblast and wrongly adds mesoderm -- neither belongs to the primary-villus stage.

questions.learning_objective: State that a primary stem villus consists of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast only.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: False statement about secondary villi
questions.question: As regards the secondary villi, all are true EXCEPT:

options.C: The do not contain fetal blood vessels
options.D: They contain a core of 2ry mesoderm
options.E: They are found in decidua basalis

explanations.A: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is TRUE). Secondary villi do retain their cytotrophoblast layer, inherited from the primary-villus trophoblast.
explanations.B: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is TRUE). Secondary villi likewise retain their syncytiotrophoblast layer.
explanations.C: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is TRUE). Secondary villi do not yet contain fetal blood vessels -- vascularisation is what marks the later, tertiary stage.
explanations.D: Correct (i.e. this statement is FALSE, the one to choose). Secondary villi contain a core of primary (1ry), not secondary (2ry), mesoderm -- this is the same terminology point tested elsewhere in this bank: extraembryonic mesoderm is itself the primary mesoderm.
explanations.E: Incorrect (i.e. this statement is TRUE). Villi, secondary included, are found projecting into the intervillous space at the placental site, anchored toward the decidua basalis.

questions.learning_objective: State that secondary villi contain a core of primary, not secondary, mesoderm.

field_notes.keySource: printed answer table p.15 row 62 = d

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Composition of a tertiary stem villus
questions.question: A tertiary stem villus consists of:

options.E: Cytotrophoblast, Syncytiotrophoblast & extraembryonic mesoderm with small blood vessels

explanations.A: Incorrect. Trophoblast alone, with no mesoderm, describes the primary-villus stage, not the tertiary (vascularised) stage.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Omitting the cytotrophoblast is wrong -- both trophoblast layers persist through all villus stages.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Omitting the syncytiotrophoblast is likewise wrong, and this option also omits the fetal blood vessels that define the tertiary stage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The mesoderm within villi is extraembryonic (primary), not intraembryonic -- intraembryonic mesoderm belongs to the embryo's own body, not the placental villi.
explanations.E: Correct. A tertiary (definitive) stem villus consists of cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast and extraembryonic mesoderm. This mesodermal core now also contains small fetal blood vessels. This is the fully vascularised, mature villus stage, the one capable of fetal-maternal gas and nutrient exchange.

questions.learning_objective: State that a tertiary stem villus consists of trophoblast, extraembryonic mesoderm and small fetal blood vessels.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Events during implantation
questions.question: During implantation, the blastocyst:

options.A: Implants in the body of the uterus
options.B: Causes a change in the endometrial tissues
options.D: Is implanted at its embryonic pole

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own (i.e. this IS true, but not the complete answer). The blastocyst does normally implant in the body of the uterus.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own (i.e. this IS true, but not the complete answer). Implantation does trigger a decidual change in the endometrial tissue.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own (i.e. this IS true, but not the complete answer). The blastocyst does implant within the endometrium.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own (i.e. this IS true, but not the complete answer). Implantation does occur at the embryonic pole, the side bearing the inner cell mass.
explanations.E: Correct. All four statements describe true events of implantation together. They cover site (uterine body), tissue response (endometrial/decidual change), and depth (embedding into the endometrium). They also cover orientation, since implantation proceeds embryonic-pole first.

questions.learning_objective: List the events of implantation together (site, endometrial change, depth, orientation).

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Correct statement about sperm capacitation
questions.question: As regards sperm capacitation, choose the CORRECT statement:

options.A: Occurs in male just before ejaculation
options.D: Prevents entrance of more than one sperm to oocyte
options.E: Removes the head of the sperm

explanations.A: Incorrect. Capacitation occurs within the female genital tract, after ejaculation, not in the male just before it.
explanations.B: Correct. Capacitation strips the glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the sperm surface. This change is a prerequisite for the acrosome reaction. Without capacitation, the sperm cannot undergo the acrosome reaction and so cannot fertilise the oocyte, making it essential for fertilisation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Capacitation is caused by exposure to secretions of the female genital tract, not by the zona pellucida, which the sperm has not yet reached during capacitation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Preventing entry of more than one sperm is the role of the zona reaction (block to polyspermy), a separate, later event -- not a function of capacitation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Capacitation strips a surface coat from the sperm; it does not remove the sperm head, which remains intact and is required for fertilisation.

questions.learning_objective: State that sperm capacitation is essential for fertilisation.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Structures the zona pellucida surrounds
questions.question: Zona pellucida surrounds:

explanations.A: Incorrect on its own (i.e. this IS true, but not the complete answer). The zona pellucida does surround the morula.
explanations.B: Incorrect on its own (i.e. this IS true, but not the complete answer). The zona pellucida does surround the zygote.
explanations.C: Incorrect on its own (i.e. this IS true, but not the complete answer). The zona pellucida does surround the early blastocyst, before hatching.
explanations.D: Incorrect on its own (i.e. this IS true, but not the complete answer). The zona pellucida is present from the primary oocyte stage onward.
explanations.E: Correct. The zona pellucida is present from the primary oocyte stage onward. It continues to surround the zygote and every cleavage stage, morula and early blastocyst alike. It disappears only later, at hatching, before implantation begins.

questions.topic: Embryology - Events of the second week
questions.learning_objective: State that the zona pellucida surrounds the conceptus from the primary oocyte through the early blastocyst.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: First two intraembryonic germ layers to differentiate
questions.question: The first 2 intraembryonic germ layers that differentiate are:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Ectoderm and endoderm are named only after third-week gastrulation; the second-week layers, formed earlier, are called epiblast and hypoblast.
explanations.B: Correct. During the second week, the inner cell mass reorganises into the bilaminar embryonic disc. The epiblast, columnar cells, faces the amniotic cavity. The hypoblast, cuboidal cells, faces the blastocoele/yolk sac, and together these are the first two germ layers to differentiate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ectoderm and mesoderm are both later, third-week gastrulation products, not the earliest second-week layers.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This mixes an early term (hypoblast) with a later one (ectoderm) -- the correct early pairing is epiblast and hypoblast together.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Like option D, this mixes a later term (endoderm) with an early one (epiblast) -- the terms should not be mixed across the two stages.

questions.learning_objective: Name epiblast and hypoblast as the first two germ layers to differentiate.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: The extraembryonic coelom
questions.question: The Extraembryonic coelom:

options.B: Is first formed in 3rd postnatal week
options.D: Is obliterated by the expansion of the placenta

explanations.A: Incorrect. The extraembryonic coelom forms within extraembryonic mesoderm itself, not as a space between the two trophoblast layers.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The extraembryonic coelom forms prenatally, during the second week -- there is no "postnatal week" in prenatal embryology, and this option misstates both the timing and the developmental stage entirely.
explanations.C: Correct. Coalescing lacunae within extraembryonic mesoderm create the extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity). This cavity is entirely lined by that same mesoderm. Its somatic layer lies against the trophoblast/amnion, while its splanchnic layer lies against the yolk sac.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The extraembryonic coelom is progressively obliterated as the amniotic cavity expands later in development, not by expansion of the placenta.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Option C correctly describes the extraembryonic coelom, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that the extraembryonic coelom is lined by extraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.subject: dev
questions.title: Development of the amniotic cavity
questions.question: The amniotic cavity develops:

options.A: Between the inner cell mass & the trophoblast

explanations.A: Incorrect per this bank's printed key (letter d is marked correct, not this option) -- though its wording is worth noting: the printed key's own remark text actually restates this option's wording ("between inner cell mass & trophoblast") rather than option d's, a letter/remark mismatch resolved here in favour of the printed letter, per house rule, with the doubt recorded rather than silently corrected.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The amniotic cavity develops on the epiblast side of the bilaminar disc, not within extraembryonic mesoderm (which instead lines the separate extraembryonic coelom).
explanations.C: Incorrect. The amniotic cavity develops on the epiblast side, adjacent to but not literally within, the inner cell mass as a whole.
explanations.D: Correct per this bank's printed key. This local answer bank marks the amniotic cavity's development to the first week after fertilisation. Most standard embryology teaching instead places this event in the second week, alongside the rest of bilaminar disc formation.
